title: The Future of Art History: Carnegie Internationals in Context - Carnegie Museums
text:
The Future of Art History: Carnegie Internationals in Context
MEMBERS EVENT
Virtual via Zoom
Tuesday, November 10, 2026
6:30–7:30 p.m
.
The term “contemporary art” was coined in the mid-20th century to describe the art of our moment or recent past. However, since 1896, Carnegie Museum of Art has exhibited and collected the art of our moment, making it one of the oldest museums in the country dedicated to “contemporary art.” But what does that mean, and how did the longest-running survey of international art come to be in Pittsburgh?
During this virtual lecture, explore how the Carnegie International, now in its 59th iteration, has informed and transformed Carnegie Museum of Art’s collection and building in remarkable ways. Gain a deeper understanding of the ground-breaking art and artists who have made lasting impacts and discover how the exhibition moved from a jury system to embracing curatorial vision.
JOIN US
Installation view of
The 1961 Pittsburgh International Exhibition of Contemporary Painting and Sculpture
, 1961, Carnegie Museum of Art

title: Terms of Use for Teen Members - Carnegie Museums
text:
Terms of Use for Teen Members
To ensure the safety and welfare of all participants, the Museum asks that Teen Members show common courtesy to fellow visitors and members and not engage in physical, verbal, or written behavior that is unsafe, illegal, violence inciting, abusive, disorderly, disruptive, hostile, or threatening to, or constitutes hate speech directed at visitors, museum staff, service providers, or others. These behaviors include, but are not limited to, hitting, kicking, biting, inappropriate touching or language, sexual harassment, and/or possessing weapons or illegal substances.
The Museum reserves the right to deny admission or remove any persons engaging in such behavior. Museum staff members may contact Security as needed. Teen members in violation of the above listed terms will have their Teen membership immediately revoked without notice.
Carnegie Museums reserves the right to change the Terms of Use for Teen Members at any time.

title: Organizational Access Membership - Carnegie Museums
text:
Organizational Access Membership
Membership for Our Community Partners
Carnegie Museums is eager to welcome organizational partners as members, free-of-charge, so they can share the joy and wonder of the four Carnegie Museums with the individuals and families they serve.
Our complimentary Organizational Access Membership is available to qualifying 501(c)(3) community-based organizations that serve underserved youth, unhoused individuals, veterans, and seniors receiving public assistance. When visiting, there must be at least one organizational staff member present with valid employment credentials, and the staff member must be accompanied by individuals served by the organization.
Each visit allows for a total of 11 people per day to any of the four Carnegie Museums. (Note: not for the personal use of an organization’s staff.)
Organizational Access Membership Benefits
:
Unlimited free general admission to Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History, Kamin Science Center, and The Andy Warhol Museum for at least 1 organizational staff member and up to 10 individuals that the nonprofit serves
Invitations to events and programming designed with a teen-centric lens
Free reciprocal admission at 300+ ASTC museums and science centers
Free reciprocal admission at an additional 250+ ROAM museums and arboretums, plus 20+ major art and natural history museums
Discounts on classes, camps, educational films at the Rangos Giant Cinema, laser shows, lectures, and special events
A 10% discount in museum stores and cafes (20% store discount during Member Shopping Days)
Free subscription to
Carnegie
magazine
10 Half-off coupons for educational films at The Rangos Giant Cinema
Apply Today!

title: Digital Membership Card - Carnegie Museums
text:
Digital Membership Card
In support of the museums’ sustainability vision, Carnegie Museums membership cards are now digital! Members will be able to download their digital membership card to their smartphone and visit their museums by simply presenting their digital membership card, a valid photo ID*, or by providing their name or email at the admissions desk.*
Have questions? Jump to our FAQ page below.
*Members may be required to present a valid photo ID for entrance.
Follow the instructions below to download and access your digital membership card.
How to Download Your Digital Membership
How to install on an
iPhone
device:
iPhones have a native app called Apple Wallet. Click the “Download” button in the email you received on your iPhone, then “Add to Wallet,” then “Add.” Your digital membership card will automatically download to the Apple Wallet app.
To access the digital wallet, swipe down on your home screen to activate the Search function. Type “Wallet” into the search bar. Then tap the Wallet icon under the “Applications” header. From there, you can access your digital card.
How to install on an
Android
device:
If you have an Android device, we recommend Google Wallet as the #1 option for Android users. Google Wallet is a native OS app that is easy to use, reliable, secure, and already pre-installed on most Android devices:
Click the “Download Membership Card” button in the email you received on your phone, then “Add to Google Wallet”. A preview will appear. Click “Save to Google Wallet”.
In some cases, Google Wallet might ask you to log in so you can save it to an account. Please log in to continue (no credit card information should be required).
The card will be saved in Google Wallet, and you can access it from the Google Wallet app at any time.
Need help installing?
Check out this FAQ from our partners at Cuseum
.
Digital Membership Card FAQ
What is a Carnegie Museums digital membership card? Is it the same as an app?
Digital membership cards are an eco-friendly alternative to mailed plastic cards. Your Carnegie Museums digital membership card is an app that can be accessed directly from your smartphone.
I have not received my digital membership card
Please complete
this survey
, and we will send your Carnegie Museums digital membership card to the email address associated with your membership.
I downloaded my card but can’t find it.
If you have an iPhone, the card will automatically download to Apple Wallet. Check the app for your new card (scroll through any cards that are already there–it may be hiding!). If you have an Android, you’ll need to download Wallet Passes from the Play Store prior to downloading the card.
My family member is also on my membership account. How can they receive the card?
iPhone/iOS- Navigate to the back of the card (tap on the “…” button on the front), then tap on the share icon at the top right to send the card to your secondary member.
Android- Navigate to the back of the card (tap on the small “i” on the front) and use the “Share Pass” button to send the card to your secondary member.
I still have a physical card that has not expired. Can I use it?
Members can present their current physical membership cards at visitor services until the expiration date on the card. Members will then have the option to check in at visitor services with their
digital card
, name, or phone number.* Patrons Circle members will continue to receive physical cards in the mail.
How do I access the back of my digital card?
iOS/iPhone
1. Open your Carnegie Museums digital membership card in your Apple Wallet.
2. Tap on the three dots at the top right of the card. If you don’t see the dots, make sure you are not accessing the card from your lock screen.
Android
1. Open your Carnegie Museums digital membership card in Google Wallet.
2. Tap on the “i” icon at the bottom right of the card.
How will my reciprocal benefits work when visiting other museums?
Digital cards for all member levels display the ASTC, while Dual-level and above also display the ROAM program logos, providing links to up-to-date lists of participating organizations in the programs. Simply show your digital card and a valid photo ID at the admissions desk (we advise you to call the participating museum you plan to visit ahead of time).
If I download my digital card, do I still need an admission ticket to visit Carnegie Museums of Art & Natural History, Kamin Science Center, or The Andy Warhol Museum?
All visits to any of the four Carnegie Museums require a ticket for admission. Though advance tickets are not required, we recommend members reserve their free member tickets in advance for quicker check-in.
I don’t want a Carnegie Museums digital membership card. What should I do?
If you don’t wish to download the card, simply disregard the message, and you won’t be offered this feature until you renew your membership. Members can visit the museums by simply presenting their digital membership card, a valid photo ID*, or by offering their name or email at the admissions desk.*
Patrons Circle members will continue to receive physical cards in the mail. If you are a Patrons Circle member and have a question, please call us at 412.622.5772.
*Members may be required to present a valid photo ID for entrance.
Can I receive a printed plastic card instead of a digital membership card?
Physical plastic cards are available only to Patrons Circle members. Digital cards can be accessed on your smartphone or printed from your home printer. We appreciate your understanding as we continue to improve your experience in our museum and deepen our commitment to reducing our environmental impact.
I don’t have a smartphone, what should I do?
Members will have the option to check in at the admissions desk with a valid photo ID* or by offering their name or email at the admissions desk.* If you wish to reserve tickets in advance, please contact us.
*Members may be required to present a valid photo ID for entrance.
I have a question about my membership information or benefits shown on my digital card.
Please contact us at
membership@carnegiemuseums.org
or 412.622.3314.

title: Carnegie Music Hall Take Your Seat! Campaign - Carnegie Museums
text:
Carnegie Music Hall Take Your Seat! Campaign
Carnegie Museums invites you to become a part of Carnegie Music Hall’s incredible history by naming a seat.
The historic renovations to our city’s iconic hall ensure that future generations will enjoy everything the space has to offer year-round and for centuries to come. Complete with a new HVAC system, accessibility features, and seating, the restoration both increases accessibility and enhances the experience of all who attend concerts, performances, or celebrations in this beautiful space. The talented teams of builders, architects, engineers, and conservators have maintained the Hall’s original splendor and kept the renowned majesty of the Music Hall preserved. Past beauty meets modern improvement in the next chapter of Carnegie Music Hall’s rich legacy!
Learn more
about the most significant renovation in Carnegie Music Hall’s 128-year history.
Your Impact
Andrew Carnegie’s dream was to create a cultural hub for Pittsburgh, stating “The success of Library, Art Gallery, Museum, and Music Hall — a noble quartet in an immense building — is one of the chief satisfactions of my life.”
The Take Your Seat!
Campaign presents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a part of Carnegie Music Hall’s incredible legacy. When you name a seat, you leave a lasting mark on one of Pittsburgh’s most iconic cultural institutions and guarantee its lasting vitality. Your support will be commemorated by an engraving of your name, or the name of someone you wish to honor, on the seat of your choice.
Note: Character limits for the plaque engravings are no more than 20 characters per line, up to three lines.
Take your seat!
Contact Beth Brown at
brownb@carnegiemuseums.org
or
412-622-8859
FAQS
What do I receive when I make a gift to Carnegie Music Hall’s
Take Your Seat
! Campaign?
Each seat donation is commemorated with a personalized, engraved brass plaque on the seat(s) you choose in Carnegie Music Hall when making your donation.
What does my gift support?
Your donation helps Carnegie Museums fulfill its vital mission to preserve and expand the resources of art and science as agents of personal growth and social advancement in Pittsburgh and beyond.
What will be on my plaque?
Each plaque has space for a max of 25 characters per line and up to 2 lines of text. You can personalize it with your name, or the name of a relative, friend, or organization. Naming must be within the character limit and is subject to the approval of Carnegie Museums.
Where will the plaque be placed? How long will the plaque be in place?
Each plaque will be centered on the back of the seat. Plaques will be placed and maintained for the usable life of the seat.
May I choose the seat?
Yes.
Will the seat I name become my seat for the events I attend in Carnegie Music Hall?
No. The
Take Your Seat!
campaign is a naming opportunity only and does not include tickets or seat assignments for performances or events. The seat may be available for reservation for a particular event on a first-come first-serve basis.
How long will it take for the plaque to be installed?
Plaques are installed on a rolling basis. After naming your seat, please give us approximately 1 month for the plaque to be engraved and then installed.
Will I be notified when my plaque is installed?
Yes. You will receive a letter at the mailing address provided at checkout informing you that your plaque has been installed.
Is purchasing a seat plaque tax deductible?
Carnegie Museums is a 501[c]3 nonprofit organization, and donations to the Carnegie Music Hall Take Your Seat! Campaign are tax-deductible to the full extent allowed by law.
A Brief 128-Year History
November 5, 1895
– The Music Hall is dedicated in addition to Carnegie Library, Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History, and the Lecture Hall. The first organ is installed, built by the Farrand & Votey Organ Company.
April 18, 1896
– 50th public organ recital, presented by Music Director Frederic Archer. Organ recitals were offered for free, twice a week. The year also marks the Art Society of Pittsburgh’s founding of the Pittsburgh Orchestra. Carnegie Music Hall acts as its home venue, and Frederic Archer is appointed Conductor.
1901
– Frederic Archer passes away. His position as Music Director is filled by Edwin H. Lemare, a nationally lauded organist. Lemare’s likeness is included in a series of Will’s Cigarettes collectible cards. These cigarette cards are the predecessor of contemporary baseball cards.
1905
– A giant, wooden fan is installed in the Music Hall to cool the space during the spring and summer.
1907
– The Oakland campus is significantly expanded to include a new dinosaur hall, the instantly recognizable foyer to the Music Hall, and Halls of Sculpture and Architecture. Newly appointed Music Director, Charles Heinroth, publicly laments the already antiquated state of the Music Hall organ and begins searching for contractors to renovate the instrument.
1910
– The original architectural design of the Music Hall changes with the removal of two exterior towers and the enclosure of the original curved entryway. The Pittsburgh Orchestra dissolves due to lack of funding. Charles Heinroth hires Herman Skinner to renovate the organ. Skinner adds several new pipes, refurbishes existing brass-work, and builds a new console.
1917
– Herman Skinner returns for additional work on the organ. Most of the original pipework is completely overhauled, and he adds several new “ranks” (rows of vertical pipes that play the same tone at different pitches). His changes are so thorough, the organ now bears his company’s name: The Ernest M. Skinner Company.
May 2, 1926
– A combination of private seed funding and public support sees the creation of the new Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra. The ensemble plays its inaugural show on this date.
April 24, 1927
– Building on public fervor for live entertainment, the Symphony’s board of directors organizes a Sunday music series. The following day, nine of the board members are arrested in violation of Pittsburgh’s Blue Laws, which banned secular music and public performances on Sundays. Ironically, some of these Blue Laws are still in place but were rendered legally unenforceable by the Supreme Court in 1978.
1933
– The Music Hall’s organ is rebuilt again, with several ranks and percussive elements added. The organ is considered one of the finest in the United States.
1936
– The first national broadcast of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra is held.
1950
– The Music Hall’s organ is renovated again. Stops, ranks, and further improvements are added.
1961
– The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra is widely considered one of the best in the country. It is the only American symphony that sells out every performance.
1981
– The last free public organ recital is held. The organ will lay mostly silent for another 29 years.
2008
– Jeanette-based organist and conservatist, Robert Copeland, completes three renovation stages of the Skinner Organ. His restoration brings the organ back to semi-working function.
2010
– The Skinner Organ is played for the Organ Historical Society’s 2010 convention in Pittsburgh. It is the last time the organ is played for the public.
2023
– Renovations start.
2024
– Renovations end.

title: Tax-smart Gifts - Carnegie Museums
text:
Tax-smart Gifts
Explore tax-smart gift options
Learn about gifts that maximize the impact of your support while providing tax benefits for you!
Stocks, securities, & mutual funds
Donate stock, securities, or mutual funds and potentially receive tax deductions while avoiding capital gains taxes.
Many people choose to give stocks, securities, or mutual funds instead of gifts of cash. Giving appreciated assets like these help you avoid paying capital gains taxes, and can give you an income tax deduction for the full value of the gift, if you’ve had the assets for more than one year.
Give appreciated assets now and enjoy the benefits, or add us as a beneficiary of these assets and eliminate estate and inheritance tax, making the most of your gift.
Benefits
Gifts of assets can often save you far more on taxes than gifts of cash
Avoid all capital gains taxes
Receive an income tax deduction for the value of the assets (if you’ve had them for more than a year)
Make an immediate impact on our mission
How it works
Transfer appreciated securities directly to us (and avoid all capital gains taxes).
Receive a tax receipt for the value of the assets.
The securities are sold and the funds put directly to use for greatest impact.
Contact us for more information
Gifts of appreciated stock or mutual fund shares may have favorable tax benefits for you. Consult your accountant or your attorney to discuss your tax situation and the advantages of making a gift of securities to Carnegie Museums. You can contact donorrelations@carnegiemuseums.org for transfer instructions. The procedure for making a gift of stock or mutual fund shares varies slightly. In both cases, please notify donorrelations@carnegiemuseums.org with the name and number of the shares that are being transferred so that we can record and acknowledge your gift as quickly as possible. The tax ID number for Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh is 25-0965280.
Qualified Charitable Distributions from your IRA
Give tax-free gifts from your IRA that benefit our mission and you.
A Qualified Charitable Distribution (QCD) is a tax-efficient way for individuals who are age 70 ½ or older to make gifts directly from their Individual Retirement Account (IRA).
QCDs can count towards satisfying an individual’s Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) for the year, which is the minimum amount that an individual must withdraw from their IRA each year once they reach age 73.
Benefits
Reduce taxable income
Counts towards your Required Minimum Distribution for the year
Make an immediate impact on our mission
How it works
Instruct your IRA custodian to distribute funds directly to one or more eligible charities.
Enjoy the benefit of a tax-free distribution from your IRA, contributing towards your required minimum distribution for the year.
Potentially reduce tax liability by excluding the distribution amount from taxable income.
You will not receive a charitable income tax deduction for a Qualified Charitable Distribution.
Contact us for more information
Gifts of real estate and art
Donate real estate or art to make a lasting impact, unlocking the hidden potential of your property’s value.
Making a gift of real estate or art to charity may be an appealing option for property owners with appreciated value, as it helps avoid capital gains tax liabilities.
Additionally, it benefits individuals seeking to simplify estate planning, reduce estate tax liability, and relieve themselves from ownership expenses and maintenance burdens.
Benefits
Eliminate ownership and maintenance expenses.
Make a significant charitable gift in support of our mission.
How it works
Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh may accept a gift of real estate after reviewing the property. Real estate may be eligible if:
You have a clear title
You have owned the property for more than one year
The property has appreciated in value
There are no environmental or other concerns
Real estate may be given either by deed during your lifetime or in your will. Seek the advice of a financial or legal advisor to see if this option is right for you and your financial goals.
Artwork and Other Items for our Collections
Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh has strict guidelines regarding the acceptance of artwork, artifacts, specimens, archives, ephemera and other items of tangible personal property. Contact us to see if your item meets our criteria and can be gifted to the Museums now or in the future.

Donate real estate in your will or trust or through a Transfer on Death (TOD) Deed to ensure it is used for a charitable purpose and not subject to potential disputes or mismanagement in the future.
Consult with a qualified estate planning attorney and a financial advisor to determine if this option is right for you.

title: Planned Giving FAQs - Carnegie Museums
text:
Planned Giving FAQs
Is my estate big enough to leave a planned gift?
Yes! Gifts of any size are deeply appreciated. Many people choose to leave a percentage of their estate, which scales up or down with your estate size.
Can my gift remain anonymous?
Yes! Knowing in advance about your intentions is quite helpful to our staff, but you are always welcome to not share your gift.
Can I edit my documents after I’m done?
Yes. You are always free to revise or update your estate plans.
Can I support all of the Museums or one specific Museum?
Yes, you can choose to make a gift that will support all four distinctive museums wherever the need is greatest at the time. OR, you can choose to support your favorite of our four museums. Feel free to name The Andy Warhol Museum, Carnegie Museum of Art, Carnegie Museum of Natural History, or Kamin Science Center in your will. All of our museums share the same Tax ID # 25-0965280.
Can I give art, artifacts or other property to Carnegie Museums through my will?
Carnegie Museums has strict acceptance guidelines around any tangible personal property–whether you are hoping to add an item to our collection, or would like to make a gift of property that can be sold to support our work. Please contact us to discuss your intentions.

title: The Need for Speed - Carnegie Magazine
text:
The Need for Speed
Kamin Science Center’s Science of Speed, Powered by Lenovo, combines the science of going fast with the thrill of on-track racing. Drivers, start your engines!
By Chris Fleisher
Carnegie Magazine
Fall 2026
Science & Nature
STEM
Print
A
There was a brief period of time when Cristobal Jofre was looking ahead to college with the intention of studying law. Then he experienced what it was like to drive fast.
“It wasn’t until maybe 2021, when I was really deep into watching Formula One and started doing go-karts, that I thought, ‘Nah, I’m going into engineering,’” says Jofre, who is 20 and lives in Imperial, Pennsylvania.
It wasn’t just the thrill of being strapped into a vehicle and going full throttle, says Jofre, now a junior engineering major at Penn State University. After joining a local go-kart league, he quickly discovered how little he actually knew about the science of going fast—the importance of track surface, tire grip, aerodynamics, weight distribution, and braking technique, and the psychology of knowing how to push a machine to its limit while confronting his own fears.
“It’s really interesting to go down through the technical points, the whole science behind racing,” he says.
They are concepts that visitors to Kamin Science Center now can discover for themselves with the opening of its most ambitious, immersive exhibition in years—Science of Speed, Powered by Lenovo.
Located in the former SportsWorks building, Science of Speed offers an experience unlike any other museum offering in the country, says Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., director of Kamin Science Center and vice president of Carnegie Museums. Featuring a multilevel indoor go-kart track with all-electric vehicles that can approach 40 miles per hour, the exhibition dives into the science of racing through on-track competition, driving simulators, educational exhibits, and artifacts from the racing industry.
Phot: Joshua Franzos
Kamin Science Center’s newest attraction also
offers an evening experience for adult racers.
To appeal to adult adventure seekers, the Science Center for the first time is offering an after-hours experience just for grown-ups. On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday evenings, adult racing enthusiasts 18 and older will have the opportunity to drive high-performance karts turned up to faster speeds than during the day, or simply relax and watch others race while enjoying light bites, craft cocktails, and local beers from the “Pit Stop” lounge.
At its core, Science of Speed is an opportunity to engage with concepts and technology that are applicable not only to world-class racers in Formula One, MotoGP, or other leagues, but also to anyone behind the wheel or looking forward to being there.
“It’s this continuous improvement process that is being driven, no pun intended, by the racing industry in their quest to just shave thousands of a second off of a lap or get another half a mile per hour on their top speed,” Brown explains. “The innovations born from this process are then showing up in our everyday lives. The car that I drive is electric, and probably three-quarters of the technology came about because, at some point in the past, some racer, a driver, an engineer, a team was like, ‘We need to try and do this.’”
Experiential Science
Kamin Science Center has long connected scientific concepts with tangible, experiential exhibits. But Science of Speed aims to reach a broader audience that includes teens and adults who want to test their mettle in high-speed electric cars.
The vehicles are centrally controlled and set differently for drivers aged 13+ during the regular daytime hours. But at night, things get faster for adults 18+ for a more competitive experience.
“The car that I drive is electric, and probably three-quarters of the technology came about because, at some point in the past, some racer, a driver, an engineer, a team was like, ‘We need to try and do this.’”
Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., Director of Kamin Science Center
Adult drivers who have been behind the wheel for decades might think they understand concepts like the interplay of friction and velocity, but learning by doing is often the best method.
“I think in many people’s cases, the more physically engaged you can be with a topic, the better, as it moves from abstraction to actual putting into practice,” Brown says. “Suddenly it becomes real. You can read about the absorption of a crash barrier for a car, but then when you’re in a go-kart and you smash into a wall at 30 miles per hour, you experience what that means.”
Craig Thomas recalls the sensation he had when he first began racing high-performance go-karts a decade ago. A professional mechanic who raced competitive motocross bikes in his youth, he discovered go-karts when applying for a mechanics job at a go-kart track in Monroeville.
When he first saw the karts, he mistakenly assumed they were the kind “like when you go to Myrtle Beach, and they’d go 10 to 12 miles per hour, just putting around.”
Then he climbed inside one and took it on a test lap.
Photo: Joshua Franzos
“They were so much faster than I thought they were,” recalls Thomas, who is now general manager of Three Rivers Karting Entertainment Park in Leetsdale, Pennsylvania. “The level of skill that I needed to be fast caught me by surprise. It was exhilarating. It reawakened my thrill for speed and going fast.”
He learned early on that going fast requires more than mashing the throttle to the floor and sliding around corners.
Counterintuitively, if you want to go fast, you need to learn how to brake.
“Braking is far more important than you’d think,” he says. “The release of the brake is probably the most important thing. In order to be fast, you have to be gradual and not treat it like an on-and-off switch.”
Effective braking relies on an understanding of friction, tire wear, weight distribution, and track surface. Knowing how and where to let up on the throttle and gradually apply the brakes, depending on severity of the turn or camber of the track, is essential. All of these concepts are not only explained through informative displays but also can be tested and analyzed at the Science Center’s newest experience.
Lessons in Performance
“There’s quite a bit of technology in the track,” Brown says.
Lessons in materials science are an important part of Science of Speed. The track surface has an epoxy coating that performs differently than the paved asphalt more familiar to everyday drivers, requiring even the most experienced racers to adjust their approach on turns as they search for grip.
“As cars drive on it, the rubber will actually come off the tires and start to create a more adhesive surface,” Brown explains. “The idea is that the kart will stick to it enough that it won’t slide and lose that energy as it goes around the corners, allowing it to go as fast as possible while maintaining its forward momentum.”
Visitors will also learn about the physical fitness required to negotiate a real race. The all-electric go-karts handle quite differently than modern automobiles, and interactive exhibits will give visitors a sense of the strength required to steer a race car.
“There’s no power steering,” Brown explains. “So, you have to be able to turn the wheel of a car that’s hurtling along and keep it on the road.”
Drivers will also be able to analyze data about their own driving. Science Center visitors who sign up for a turn on the track will create a racer profile that records their performance data, including lap times and top speeds. They can then track their progress as they hone their skills on repeat attempts.
“Drivers will have the data from their own races to be able to study what they were doing and what they weren’t,” Brown says.
Data analysis is how Rick Shank is hoping to improve his own track performance. The 46-year-old IT professional has been racing for over two decades and currently competes in a league at Three Rivers Karting. He collects as much data as he can, matching lap times to the different karts he drives every week to figure out how to maximize his performance on each machine. And he’s relishing the opportunity to expand his dataset on the Science Center’s track.
“I am looking for consistency. I’m looking for which karts are working for me, which ones come up to speed fast,” he says. “How do I crack this nut, from a math side? I look at the data.”
Off-Track Learning
Shank understands that racing is as much about mental preparation as it is the mech-anics of the kart. That’s the component that he believes he needs to improve on the most.
“Honestly, what holds me back a lot is the psychology component of racing,” he says.
He took the pole position in one recent race with the fastest lap time, but halfway through the 10-lap competition he went from first to worst.
“This was 100% race craft,” he says. “I left a lane open. People behind me realized and capitalized on it.”
But you don’t have to join the action on track to learn about the mental side of racing in Science of Speed. These concepts can also be tested in five fully immersive simulators.
“They were so much faster than I thought they were. The level of skill that I needed to be fast caught me by surprise. It was exhilarating. It reawakened my thrill for speed and going fast.”
Craig Thomas, general manager of Three Rivers Karting Entertainment Park
One simulator is dedicated to Formula One, giving users a virtual sensation of what it’s like to take hot laps on famous circuits around the world. Meanwhile, four other simulators are interconnected so visitors can go head-to-head in competition and learn more about the craft of executing a pass or defending against someone coming up behind them. Each simulator turns lessons about external forces, control, and decision-making into a visceral, real-time test of speed and skill.
“Every part of this experience is designed to turn concepts in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics into something physical, competitive, exciting—and, most importantly, unforgettable,” Brown says.
Science of Speed offers plenty of other off-track experiences for anyone not interested in the thrill of competition. A “wind-tunnel” exhibit allows users to examine the aerodynamics of differently shaped vehicles, comparing the streamline of an SUV, for example, to an open-wheel race car or a motorcycle.
“As you turn the wind up, you’ll be able to understand how the aerodynamics work with the way the air moves around the object, but also how it creates downforce to keep the car on the road,” Brown says.
Gearheads will get to explore the mechanics of an internal combustion engine by way of a marquee attraction that will be familiar to fans of Marvel movies: the high-performance, orange Audi R8 famously driven by Iron Man Tony Stark, with an “exploded” engine so that each component is visible.
Memorabilia from racing history is also part of Science of Speed. A lemon-colored 1959 race car known as “Ol’ Yaller,” built by California hot rod legend Max Balchowsky, is on display, as well as a signed racing suit from reigning MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez, a Ducati racing motorcycle, and racing helmets donated by the exhibition sponsor Lenovo.
And finally, those who are more interested in watching the action on track can relax in the Pit Stop lounge. Located in an open mezzanine overlooking the exhibition, the lounge introduces an entirely new type of social experience at the Science Center­—one that connects it with the other entertainment venues on the North Shore, says Megan McKenzie, director of marketing for the Science Center.
“We’re in this unique entertainment hub,” McKenzie says. “We have the casino on one side, Acrisure Stadium, PNC Park, Stage AE, and so many other major attractions right around us. We want to be part of that energy and be a place people think about visiting when they’re coming into Pittsburgh for a big event.”
The facility’s dynamic, nighttime look reflects that, with an exterior illuminated by three rails of ever-changing LED lights serving as a beacon to visitors.
“I think it’s going to be its own best advertisement,” Brown professes.
For local race fans, the attraction is the concept itself. Brown says that Science of Speed will invite competitive karting leagues to race there, opening up opportunities to bring the region’s racing community into the heart of the city. Nothing else like this exists so close to downtown.
“I love the idea that it becomes more accessible to more people,” says Shank. “Anytime I can get some additional practice on a different style of track, it not only benefits the region but, personally, I’ll enjoy that a lot.”
For Jofre, the Penn State engineering student, Science of Speed is the perfect marriage of his personal passion and career ambition: a place where he can test the theories of fluid dynamics, the friction coefficient, and other lessons he’s learning in class as he prepares (hopefully) to build cars professionally for a racing team.
Sure, racing is fun. But it’s also serious science.
Science of Speed is Powered by Lenovo, with support from Racing Partner: PPG.

title: Reel Revival - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Reel Revival
Carnegie Museum of Art’s Film Series mines a rich archive and carries forward the avant-garde tradition of the museum’s film programming.
By Justin Hopper
Fall 2026
Art
Print
A
Screening of Golden Jubilee (Suneil Sanzgiri, 2021, 19 min.), 2024 Carnegie Museum of Art Film Series, programmed by Astria Suparak, Nov. 30, 2024; photo: Zachary Riggleman / Carnegie Museum of Art
As part of this year’s
Carnegie Museum of Art Film Series
, coinciding with the 59th Carnegie International, the museum invited Rwandan filmmaker Kivu Ruhorahoza to engage with its theater and film collections. His selections, as he says, “document struggle and celebrate resilience, creativity, and hope”—whether that’s what’s shown on the screen or what has gone into the making of the work.
The works that he’s chosen feature stories and directors from around the globe, and span five decades of filmmaking. And though the annual Film Series is in just its fourth year, its ambitions to tell innovative, expansive stories build on a much longer film history.
Since 1970, the museum’s collection and curation of film, video, and time-based artworks have broken new ground. Indeed, the Museum of Art was one of the first American museums to create a film department. “Now, we’re at a moment of revisiting the collection, so it’s been fruitful to think about how film, video, and [related] installation work can become part of this richer, wider dialogue,” says Liz Park, Richard Armstrong Curator of Contemporary Art at the Carnegie Museum of Art.
The Film Series was begun in 2023 to be in dialogue with the museum’s collection of nearly 1,000 films and video pieces, and to hand over the reins to artists and allow them freedom to create programming that works from their point of view.
For this year’s series, Ruhorahoza has selected international films that unearth and portray complex and hidden histories of resistance, in parallel with the Carnegie International’s similar themes.
“I wanted to honor and celebrate the human spirit under immense pressure,” says Ruhorahoza. “The precariousness of employment, of housing; the fragility of negotiated peace between belligerent forces; the precariousness of health and, ultimately, of life itself. In an age marked by seemingly unstoppable forces intent on eroding human dignity, forces amplified by overwhelming technological power, and political cynicism, I wanted to celebrate stories of quiet, individual, and collective defiance.”
Rubaiyat Hossain,
Made in Bangladseh
(film still), 2019; courtesy of Rubaiyat Hossain
For example, Kaori Oda’s hybrid documentary
Gama
explores a landscape of deep historical trauma in Japan, delving into the Okinawan caves in which civilians hid from the World War II battle above—and where many of them died.
Workingman’s Death
by Austrian filmmaker Michael Glawogger documents hazardous labor in far-flung parts of the world: miners in Ukraine and butchers in Nigeria; Chinese steel workers and Indonesian sulfur workers. And fiction films such as Lizzie Borden’s
Born in Flames
and Rubaiyat Hossain’s
Made in Bangladesh
tell stories about disparate places in which people come together through work and community to push for transformation.
While Ruhorahoza’s series is drawn mostly from the artist’s experiences of international film rather than from Carnegie Museum of Art’s collections, his choices are in line with the common themes running through the Film Series screenings at the museum over recent years, including work, community, and experimentation—and, as Ruhorahoza puts it, “resisting amnesia.”
“These works insist on remembering,” he says. “They preserve experiences that power would often prefer to erase. They ask us not only to witness the past but to carry it forward.”
In 2023, Pittsburgh filmmaker Tony Buba curated a series of films about work, place, and social transformation. In 2024, curator and artist Astria Suparak showed dozens of films by artists from around the world, and in 2025, Garrett Bradley reimagined the museum’s collection as a rhythm alternating between “the tactile grit of our earthly condition” and something more sublime. For 2026, the selection is expansive in its international reach and resonates with the rich and diverse history of films shown at the museum.
“We’re revisiting our incredible history of film presentation at the museum,” says Park. “And there’s many ways that the museum can do that—the Film Series is just one.”
A Rich Legacy
Sally Dixon knew that Pittsburgh was the right place for film in 1970 when she began the Department of Film, which remained its own entity until it was absorbed into modern and contemporary art in 2003. In 1973, Dixon remarked in an interview with
Carnegie
magazine that filmmakers’ “whole life is seeing. Their art, their business, is seeing. … The textures [of Pittsburgh] thrill them.”
Dixon, who died in 2019, would go on to become one of America’s most important advocates for experimental cinema and filmmakers, with a legacy that stretched far beyond Pittsburgh. In the 2022 documentary
Experimental Curator: The Sally Dixon Story
on PBS, film professor Ben Ogrodnik says, “Dixon is important because she’s a filmmaker-maker. … She was an enabler.” In Dixon’s obituary,
Art Insider
magazine referred to her as “one of the foremost voices for experimental changes in the art world,” having been one of the major forces bringing avant-garde film and video into established institutions. And that legacy was begun by her early work at the Museum of Art.
Robert Haller, Sally Dixon with Mike Chikiris taking photograph, 1975,
© Robert Haller. Made available by permission.
Until around 1970, avant-garde and experimental film were the purview of coastal megalopolises—the Film-Makers’ Cooperative in New York City and Canyon Cinema and Pacific Film Archive in San Francisco were all but the only major centers for experimental cinema work. But a postindustrial revolution was stirring, and between 1969 and 1972, the New York City film scene inspired a new focus on film as an experimental art form in unlikely places: the upstate New York cities of Binghamton and Buffalo, which paired faltering factory economies with booming universities, and—of course—Pittsburgh.
“The idea was really adventurous since there was no way of knowing what the reaction to such a program would be. Mr. Arkus has given me the freedom to shape the program as I see fit. … It’s difficult for me to imagine a more interesting job.”
Sally Dixon, Founder of the Museum of Art’s Department of Film, to
Carnegie
magazine in 1973
Dixon was one of the artists who’d fallen under the spell of New York City film missionary Jonas Mekas, founder of the Film-Makers Cooperative and, in 1970, the Anthology Film Archives. Fortunately for her, so had Leon Arkus, director of Carnegie Museum of Art. Arkus thought it was the right time and place for an official Film Section at the museum; Dixon had programmed some film events there already, and was given freedom to shape the vision for the new section—and, perhaps more importantly, a budget to make it happen.
“The idea was really adventurous since there was no way of knowing what the reaction to such a program would be,” Dixon told
Carnegie
magazine in 1973. “Mr. Arkus has given me the freedom to shape the program as I see fit. … It’s difficult for me to imagine a more interesting job.”
She immediately set to work creating one of the key nodes on the eastern U.S. film circuit. Dixon programmed screenings beginning with a series of seminal and avant-garde films from 1905 onward and an animation festival to coincide with the
1970
Pittsburgh International Exhibition of Contemporary Art
. She also created open screenings for Pittsburgh-area filmmakers to show their work; and, most importantly, she launched a series of visiting-artist screenings and talks.
Beginning with Mekas, comprising abstract animator Robert Breer and experimentalist Stan Brakhage, the Museum of Art’s burgeoning film program brought artists to Pittsburgh whose work was important to the art form, regardless of how palatable it was to larger audiences. For example, in a 1971 letter to Dixon, filmmaker Hollis Frampton bemoans the fact that the work of colleague Ken Jacobs fell flat with the audience in Pittsburgh, saying that Jacobs’ lengthy, slow
Tom, Tom the Piper’s Son
“sorts the sheep from the goats. You gotta love film [underlined three times] to dig it.” (Dixon’s taste prevailed: Not only was
Tom, Tom
acquired by the museum for its permanent collection, it is today considered one of experimental cinema’s most important artworks and is included in the National Film Registry.)
In the Theater and Beyond It
A decade ago, former museum archivist Emily Davis worked for more than a year and a half on organizing, describing, and digitizing Carnegie Museum of Art’s time-based collection, which includes the film department’s huge archive of posters, letters, videos, and audio recordings. For her, one of the most important moments in the department’s history came in 1974. Arkus oversaw the development of the Scaife Galleries, and Dixon was able to get a purpose-built theater included for showing experimental films.
“Sally made sure that [Museum of Art] theater was perfect for the art form,” says Davis, now an archivist at Carnegie Mellon University. “From the thick velvet curtains that can change with various aspect ratios, to the booth that allowed for seamless multiprojector pieces.”’
It became a place where filmmakers, both little known and with global renown, would view and discover innovative art.
Pittsburgh’s Buba was at the start of his career when the section was building up steam. Today he’s a figure known nationally and internationally for his hard-hitting yet funny hybrid documentaries about his hometown of Braddock, Pennsylvania. But in the early 1970s, Buba was an aspiring filmmaker with little to work with.
Photo: Sean Eaton
In 2023, Carnegie Museum of Art launched a new Film Series with an inaugural lineup of 17 films, programmed by the internationally acclaimed filmmaker Tony Buba. Photo: Sean Eaton
Audience at May Day screening at Carnegie Museum of Art (circa 1975).
“Sally Dixon used to do a May Day screening,” says Buba, who is still making films at 82. “You’d just bring stuff up, like an open house, and I would come and show my films. But then, in 1980, Werner Herzog was there, and I get this phone call from the museum saying, ‘Hey, Herzog’s in town and wants to see local filmmakers’ films. Can you get over here?”’
The illustrious German auteur was meant to see just 5 minutes of Buba’s 25-minute
Sweet Sal
. But not only did he demand to finish it, he also sent Buba out to get all of his work—and took the “Bard of Braddock” to breakfast the next day.
“He was really praising my work, and then Bill [Judson, Dixon’s successor from the later 1970s onward] offered me my own screening, which ended up being incredibly successful, and it really kicked off my career on the museum circuit.”
Poster for visiting filmmaker Tony Buba’s film Sweet Sal at Museum of Art Theater, 1980.
In a similar manner, today’s Film Series creates a space where filmmakers and film fans can experience works from the avant-garde to the simply little-screened; films that bring artists and artistry back to the center of screenings by giving filmmakers control over the series.
“Sally Dixon used to do a May Day screening. You’d just bring stuff up, like an open house, and I would come and show my films.”
Tony Buba, filmmaker
“Each of the filmmakers curating the series is really distinct in their style and approach,” says Park. “They bring something unique to their relationship with moving images as a resource.”
“For example, Astria Suparak screened more than 50 films over seven events, which is really ambitious,” adds Blaine Siegel, public programs manager for the museum.
Documentary shorts from the 1920s can combine with European experimentalists and Pittsburgh filmmakers from across the years.
From its establishment in the 1970s onward, the museum’s Department of Film was buying new work from independent filmmakers, establishing a collection of national prominence. Films such as Jacobs’
Tom, Tom,
Brakhage’s
Pittsburgh Trilogy
, and Carolee Schneemann’s
Fuses
—among the most influential films in American experimental cinema history—are all part of the Museum of Art’s permanent collection.
The four-year-old Film Series has drawn extensively upon those pieces in the museum’s rich archive.
“We were very clear about wanting to have filmmakers who could look at our history, our collection, and also bring what they want to see to our theater,” says Park. “I think that is part of our larger ethos of really centering artists and listening to artists. In fact, in the third year, we invited Garrett Bradley, who pulled almost entirely from our collection of films and video.”
The choice of Buba to kick off the series in 2023 was in line with this idea, says Siegel.
“Having the distance now of the first three series, I almost see Tony as an artwork,” he says, referencing Buba’s status in the Pittsburgh film community and long history with the museum’s film section. “So what if an artwork from the collection came to life and chose the work that responds to them, and then that’s how the programming happened?”
Collaboration and Videos
Judson’s tenure as head of the Film Section (1975-2003) came with new ideas. Having been Dixon’s protege, he continued her work with visiting filmmakers and screenings, but expanded the project to include video. In 1981, the museum debuted its first video-specific gallery for installation works with an exhibition by Israeli video artist Buky Schwartz titled
Videoconstructions
. The stage was set for incorporating gallery-installed video pieces into the permanent display.
Soon the museum was at the forefront of museum exhibition of video art, a medium that, in the late 1970s and 1980s, was still finding its footing with serious art audiences and collectors. In 1988, Judson secured National Endowment for the Arts funding to create a groundbreaking exhibition of American landscape video artists,
American Landscape Video: The Electronic Grove
, which not only pushed the medium forward but also paved the way for an attitude of installation work that informs the new Film Series, nearly 40 years later.
Following in the footsteps of Dixon and Judson, the museum continues to commission and facilitate new work from film and video artists. In 2023, New York City-based artist Amie Siegel used recently unearthed 16 mm film from Carnegie Museum of Natural History as well as objects from the collection in a relationship born of the museum’s purchase of another of her works a decade ago.
“Amie was invited on a research trip to the museum, and she saw all these incredible reels of film documenting scientific expeditions that the Natural History Museum scientists conducted,” says Park. “She selected and digitized expedition films to create a new work called
Panorama
, which we showed as a Forum Series exhibition in 2023, and then acquired into our collection.”
The 59th Carnegie International presents a range of time-based media. This includes Wu Tsang’s
on our way to the general strike
, on view in the museum’s Hall of Architecture, and Kearra Amaya Gopee’s
minor demons
. Both works were made specifically for the International.
The Film Series includes these kinds of works in some of its screenings, too.
Installation view of Cauleen Smith, My Caldera, 2022, single-channel, digitized 35mm film, and sound; Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh, A. W. Mellon Acquisition Endowment Fund, 2024.5; photo: Zachary Riggleman / Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh
For example, as part of the 2025 series, Bradley chose to include Cauleen Smith’s installation work
My Caldera
. On display in the Scaife Galleries, Smith’s piece plays with the whole history of time-based artwork. It projects images of volcanoes that began life as TikTok video stills, which Smith then printed frame by frame onto 35 mm film and then rendered as 4K video. Just as Smith’s artwork demands the movement between analog and digital, its presentation cannot be in a theater.
“Our gallery attendants took everyone from the theater, moved through the museum at night in total quiet to experience the work, and then back to the theater for the other screenings,” says Siegel. “It was a discussion between us and Garrett asking, ‘How do we activate this artwork? How can we make it all part of the same series, despite being this different medium?’”
Reactivating Film
In 2003, the original film and video department was folded into the contemporary art department as part of institution-wide cost-cutting measures, leading to Judson’s departure. Its screenings and artist visits became part of a broader range of work. For Davis, the former archivist, the department and its associated screenings series were essential to Pittsburgh’s experimental film and video scene.
“The Carnegie program was at the nexus of the film scene in Pittsburgh,” says Davis. “When it shut down, it was a huge blow to Pittsburgh, but also nationally—
I’ve met programmers from all over North America who would look to Bill Judson’s work for inspiration.”
The museum’s approach to reactivating its Film Series today is simple: to continue to center the work of artists, and the ideas of artists, in both the curation and the screening of time-based artworks, at a time when film and screening options are changing rapidly.
Here or There, Workshop 7: Carnegie Museum of Art Film Series, film manipulation workshop facilitated by Pittsburgh Sound + Image, Carnegie Museum of Art (Nov. 10, 2025); photo: Zachary Riggleman / Carnegie Museum of Art
“Film, as it used to be presented, is undergoing a lot of changes,” says Park. “With streaming services and cinemas no longer being as viable of businesses, we’ve seen in Pittsburgh the closing of many venues. But there’s still a strong desire among people here to gather in person at a screening—to be part of that experience together.”
As part of the International, Ruhorahoza’s installment of the Film Series focuses on themed international films rather than on the collections of the museum.
“I wanted the program to resonate with the remarkably diverse exhibition curated by Liz Park, Ryan Inouye, and Danielle A. Jackson,” says Ruhorahoza. “Although the films were selected independently, I was struck by the many unexpected conversations that emerged between them and the exhibition. Together, they create a broader reflection on memory, resilience, and the ways artists continue to confront history and imagine different futures.”
Whether tied to the International, to the collections, or simply to the remarkable spaces and artists accessible by the museum, the Film Series helps make works that might never otherwise be screened in Pittsburgh come alive.
“Liz Park and [Blaine] Siegel—I think they wanted somebody with Pittsburgh name recognition to kick it off, and I was really excited to do it because it just fills a gap,” says Buba. “There’s so many films out there you can’t see anywhere else. Last month I went to see
[West Indies: The Fugitive Slaves of Liberty]
in the current series, and it was just amazing. Because without something like this, there just isn’t a lot of alternative cinema getting shown.”

title: Shaping Pittsburgh’s Next Generation of Creatives  - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Shaping Pittsburgh’s Next Generation of Creatives
At The Andy Warhol Museum, paid fellowships provide a path to become a filmmaker or digital content creator.
By Aakanksha Agarwal
Carnegie Magazine
Fall 2026
Art
Behind the Scenes
Community
Warhol
Print
A
The video reel opens on a bartender, Herminio Ramirez, as he slides a platter of cod ceviche tostadas to his “customer,” Dahlia Saenz. She raises a watermelon basil margarita toward the camera before the reel cuts between sizzling fajitas, warm tortillas, and playful exchanges in Spanish and English. Along the way, they talk about Cinco de Mayo while showcasing Mexican holiday specials.
The finished video lasts less than a minute. Creating it took weeks of research, creative strategy, filming, and editing.
It became the centerpiece of Saenz’s capstone project for
The Warhol Academy’s Digital Content Creation Fellowship
, one of two paid fellowship tracks offered each spring and fall through The Andy Warhol Museum’s Pop District initiative. The digital content fellowship trains emerging marketers, storytellers, and content creators to develop strategic campaigns and social media for real-world clients, while the filmmaking fellowship immerses aspiring directors and documentarians in collaborative film production.
Saenz created the video reel as an online marketing campaign for Camino, the Shadyside restaurant where she worked as a hostess and a server after moving to Pittsburgh from Texas for college. Rather than inventing a hypothetical client, she built it for a place—and people—she already knew.
Over four months this spring, she joined 15 other fellows—eight in digital content creation and eight in filmmaking—who each received a $3,000 stipend, mentorship from working creative professionals, access to The Pop District’s studios and equipment, and the opportunity to produce portfolio-ready work.
Photo: Camila Casas
Fellows at The Warhol Academy become active participants in Pittsburgh’s creative community.
Kristin Hanne, director of adult workforce development programming at the Academy, calls the fellowships “inherently Warholian,” designed around embracing the curiosity that defined Andy Warhol himself. Warhol’s career was built on experimentation and collaboration across disciplines, she notes.
“A lot of industries can be rigid—this is the way, this is how you climb the ladder, and that’s the only option,” Hanne says. “But creative work isn’t just about finding the right path. It’s about having the curiosity to make one.”
A Process
As Saenz refined her presentation with digital fellowship coordinator Erin Davis and other fellows, she decided to make the same presentation to her employer. She polished the presentation with the help of her mother, translated it into Spanish, and pitched the same ideas to the owners of Camino, part of the Mas Taco restaurant group.
Hanne recalls the presentation. “She was pitching it to us, but she was also pitching it to them,” Hanne says. “She basically said, ‘I think I can do this, and here’s why.’ She showed them what she could do.”
By the time the fellowship ended, Saenz had been hired to oversee marketing and social media for all four Mas Taco restaurants.
Davis says the promotion wasn’t the result of a lucky break. “Dahlia came in very creative and ready to learn,” she notes. “What she really learned was how to structure that creativity so she could execute her vision with clarity and high-quality tactics.”
Apply for a fellowship!
That progression—from creativity to professional practice—is one Hanne says The Warhol Academy hopes to see again and again. The goal isn’t simply to teach emerging creatives how to use cameras or edit videos, she explains, but to give them the experience and confidence to turn creative ambition into sustainable work.
The Academy provides a pathway for people who might think a career in filmmaking or digital content creation is closed to them. Hanne says she isn’t necessarily looking for straight-A film students, but rather curious people with enough technical know-how to grow together.
“There isn’t one way to learn, and there isn’t one way to work,” Hanne says. “This is for anyone who wants to be involved in the arts and is inspired by everything the museum provides.”
Photo: Camila Casas
The cohorts mix filmmakers, photographers, marketers, actors, and self-taught creators. Applicants complete portfolio reviews, technical interviews, and in-person conversations before joining the program. Before classes begin, they sharpen their Adobe Premiere skills, get comfortable with the museum’s equipment, and gain access to professional gear, studio space, flexible lab hours, and, when needed, transportation assistance.
Davis, who previously worked at the National Institutes of Health, brings an operational mindset to digital storytelling. Before diving into content creation, she asked the fellows “to explain exactly what they’re making, who it’s for, and why it matters.” From the first week, fellows pitched concepts to one another, defended their creative choices, identified weaknesses, and revised their plans before production began.
“They are expected to show up prepared to explain how they will execute before they ever pick up a camera or write a script,” Davis says. “The biggest change is always an increase in operational confidence. Most people struggle to make content because their process is chaotic.” So she emphasizes the importance of preproduction planning, arguing that careful preparation allows creators to focus on stronger visuals, cleaner audio, and more intentional storytelling once production begins.
By the end of the fellowship, projects that once took participants weeks to complete can often be produced in a day. Just as important, fellows leave with stronger soft skills—confidence, public speaking, and the ability to pitch ideas to clients or employers.
Saenz recognized that shift in her own work. “I knew how to make something visually interesting,” she says. “I wanted to understand how to make something effective, and see the bigger picture—the strategy behind digital storytelling, the metrics behind advertising, and how creative work can genuinely help a business or organization.”
Collaboration
While digital content creators learned to think strategically, filmmakers learned to think collectively.
“It takes a village to make a film,” says Dan Finegold, filmmaking fellowship coordinator. “People watch a movie and think about the director, but filmmaking is one of the most collaborative art forms there is.”
A Pittsburgh native, Finegold spent more than a decade making documentaries, commercial films, and branded content before joining The Warhol Academy. For him, the fellowship is also a way to restore part of Pittsburgh’s filmmaking ecosystem. Finegold credits the now-defunct Pittsburgh Filmmakers with giving generations of artists a place to learn, borrow equipment, and build creative relationships. “The Academy isn’t exactly the same, and it’s not as large,” he says, “but it fills some of that void that Pittsburgh lost.”
That philosophy shapes the fellowship from the first week. Wednesdays focus on filmmaking fundamentals—camera systems, lighting, sound, and storytelling—while Fridays function as working labs, where fellows edit projects, borrow equipment, collaborate on productions, and learn from visiting producers, cinematographers, production designers, and other industry professionals.
“There isn’t one way to learn, and there isn’t one way to work. This is for anyone who wants to be involved in the arts and is inspired by everything the museum provides.”
Kristin Hanne, director of adult workforce development programming, The Warhol Academy
Before anyone directs a film of their own, the cohort makes one together. This spring, the filmmaking fellows profiled McKeesport glass artist Jaime Guerrero. Rather than assigning fixed roles, Finegold asked each fellow what they wanted to learn. Some operated cameras, others recorded sound, managed lighting, assisted production, or edited. As they progressed, those responsibilities rotated, giving every fellow experience across a professional film set before they led a project of their own.
Only then did fellows begin their individual work: first a short documentary about another fellow, then a 7-minute personal film. There are few creative restrictions. “I call it film camp,” Finegold says. “I’m not going to tell you what to make. You can make anything you want. I’m here to support you and help you make it as good as it can possibly be.”
No two films in the final showcase looked alike, Finegold notes.
Reilly McKay joined the program hoping to turn his passion for narrative filmmaking into a career. His film began as a public service announcement about a missing Girl Scout before veering into absurdist horror-comedy.
McKay expected to leave a stronger writer and director. Instead, he discovered that “filmmaking begins long before anyone calls ‘action.’” Storyboards, shot lists, and production schedules became just as critical as the shoot itself, while rotating through camera, sound, lighting, and production roles revealed how every decision depends on careful preparation.
“I think filmmaking is kind of like a magic trick,” McKay says. “You’re seeing the finished illusion. But if you pull back the curtain, like in
The Wizard of Oz
, you suddenly see all the gears and moving parts that make everything work.”
By the time he directed his own production—with a large cast, multiple locations, and a full crew—Finegold says McKay had grown into the role of a filmmaker responsible not only for the story but also for guiding the people bringing it to life.
“From the moment Reilly pitched the idea for the film he ultimately delivered, he stayed true to that original vision,” Finegold says. “You could feel that growth on set. Watching everyone collaborate together really showed the kind of leader Reilly had become.”
The Community
Gabriella Valdivieso was a budding filmmaker when she moved to Pittsburgh from Vermont a year ago, but she knew almost no one in the city’s arts scene. She hoped The Warhol Academy fellowship would help hone her skills while building creative connections.
“I was thrilled when I got accepted,” she says, “because it immediately felt like such a unique opportunity.”
For her documentary, Valdivieso turned to Pittsburgh’s drag community. Growing up queer, she’d long admired drag through live performances and documentaries such as
Paris Is Burning
, but wanted to tell a story rooted in her adopted city.
“What really struck me was how much variety there was,” she says. “There’s no single way to do drag in Pittsburgh.”
She was especially drawn to performers who embraced comedy and what they affectionately called “bad drag”—not poor performance, but an intentionally welcoming style that makes space for newcomers without elaborate costumes or large budgets.
That spirit carried into the production itself. Most of the short documentary was filmed over two nights in a crowded bar with a single camera. “You still have to figure out how to make everything work within the realities of production,” she says.
Finegold watched her confidence grow as the program progressed. “When she first started the fellowship, she was pretty quiet,” he says. “Then she came back with this documentary that balanced humor, chaos, and genuine emotion.”
The experience gave Valdivieso more than a finished documentary, she says. Many of the performers attended its premiere at The Warhol in June, and she later reunited with them at a Pride event while planning another community screening. “For someone who moved here without knowing many people,” she says, “that feeling of finding both a filmmaking community and a broader creative community has been really meaningful.”
Hanne says these relationships are as central as the curriculum itself. “The fellows come in thinking about projects,” she says. “They leave thinking about people.”
The Possibilities
The Academy follows what happens long after the fellowship ends, Hanne notes. “Do alumni find work? Do they continue making things? Do they hire one another? Increasingly, the answer is yes.”
One former fellow, Jackie Mishol, developed a documentary during the program that later won Best Documentary at the West Virginia Mountaineer Short Film Festival.
Alexis Cathie, another alumnus, found herself reclaiming her career path. An executive assistant turned communications manager at Catapult Greater Pittsburgh, Cathie taught herself photography, video, and social media on the job. Just before the fellowship began, she was laid off.
Instead of derailing her plans, the timing gave her clarity. “In a lot of ways, that’s where I discovered my career,” Cathie says. “I actually just turned 40, and for most of my life, I had simply worked jobs. This was different.”
Working with Davis, she refined her production process, learned techniques like retention editing, strengthened her on-camera confidence, and began thinking beyond individual pieces of content to a larger creative strategy.
“I already had plenty of ideas before the fellowship,” she says. “What The Academy gave me was the ‘how.’”
“It takes a village to make a film. People watch a movie and think about the director, but filmmaking is one of the most collaborative art forms there is.”
Dan Finegold, filmmaking fellowship coordinator
Today, she runs a creative consultancy that helps artists, entrepreneurs, and small businesses tell their stories, while also operating a formalwear brand, IMIHI, for plus-size women.
Davis says this reinforces why the fellowship emphasizes process over platforms. Social media trends and technology are always going to change, Davis says. What doesn’t change, she says, is the ability to solve problems creatively. “If people understand strategy, storytelling, and process, they’ll be able to adapt, no matter what platform comes next.”
To date, 92 individuals have graduated from the fellowship programs since they were piloted in 2021. After every cohort, alumni stay in touch through the messaging platform Slack, where they post freelance opportunities, ask for crew help, announce screenings, and share jobs. This year, The Warhol Academy hosted its first alumni gathering, bringing together fellows from every cohort since the pilot program.
“That’s a huge part of what we’re trying to do here,” Hanne says. “To make sure there’s a continuing ecosystem for people to come back to.”
Finegold says success isn’t measured by showcase night or even by the jobs fellows land afterward. It’s when they begin seeing themselves as peers in Pittsburgh’s creative community.
“My hope is that they become my colleagues,” he says. “If they leave here making stronger films, getting into festivals, and building careers as filmmakers, then I feel like I’ve done my job.”
Support for The Warhol Academy is provided by PPG Foundation, Howmet Aerospace Foundation, The Buhl Foundation, and Highmark.
