title: Tackling Climate Change, Inside and Out - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Tackling Climate Change, Inside and Out
How Carnegie Museums is taking on the global climate crisis through research, public engagement, and improving its own buildings.
By Holden Slattery
Fall 2026
Science & Nature
Print
A
On a warm June evening, about 70 residents from across Allegheny County packed a public office building in Downtown Pittsburgh to learn more about what their elected officials planned to do about climate change.
The county was seeking input on its first-ever Climate Action Plan, which when unveiled this November will lay out strategies to eliminate millions of tons of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted locally into the atmosphere each year.
But conversations about climate change can be politically charged, emotional, and complicated by scientific jargon. And so, county officials turned to Carnegie Museum of Natural History, where staff have years of experience talking about this issue within the museum and, increasingly, outside in other community settings.
Photo: John Schisler
Allegheny County officials sought the help of Carnegie Museum of Natural History as it took its Climate Action Plan to the community at public events.
“One of the hard things about talking about climate change is that a lot of folks are either resistant to discussions around it or they just don’t connect with it,” says Brittany Prischak, director of the county’s Department of Sustainability. “The Museum of Natural History is helping us take the language of climate change and bring it to regular folks.”
As the museum’s curator of Anthropocene studies, Nicole Heller has spent her career researching the impact that humans are having on the planet. And in recent years, she’s also worked to understand how to better communicate those ideas to the public. For over a decade, the Museum of Natural History has made it a priority to converse with residents about climate change outside the museum’s walls. Across town on the North Shore, its sister museum, Kamin Science Center, aims to be a town square for community dialogue on the science behind climate change and other issues.
I think museums are seen as trusted sources of information because they are embedded in communities, they work with communities, but they also put careful research into everything they do.
Mandi Lyon, program manager for schools and groups, Carnegie Museum of Natural History
In a polarized cultural and political climate, museums are one of the few institutions that have maintained a high level of trust among the public. According to the National Awareness, Attitudes, and Usage Study, an overwhelming majority of Americans—76%—consider museums to be trustworthy institutions, more than daily newspapers (60%), nongovernmental organizations (60%), and the federal government (54%).
“I think museums are seen as trusted sources of information because they are embedded in communities, they work with communities, but they also put careful research into everything they do,” says Mandi Lyon, program manager for schools and groups at Carnegie Museum of Natural History.
Education and Outreach
Since its inception, the Museum of Natural History has been a place for researchers to advance their understanding of the natural world and convey that work through exhibitions and programming.
Heller’s research has informed several exhibitions—notably
We Are Nature: Living in the Anthropocene
, which opened in 2017, and a follow up to that exhibition several years ago,
We Are Nature: A New Natural History
, with each highlighting humans’ role as an integral part of nature.
In May, Kamin Science Center unveiled
Our Place in a Changing Climate
, an exhibition that connects concepts around climate change with actual examples from western Pennsylvania. The exhibition is the proof of concept for the Science Center’s Rapid Science Engagement Initiative (RSEI)—a pilot program created to move the museum toward being more responsive to current science topics that affect daily life. Surveys and discussions with visitors and community members identified climate change as the No. 1 science topic of interest, so the Science Center chose it as the focus of the first RSEI exhibition, which occupies part of the third floor.
“If you show how it’s affecting our own communities—weather patterns, daily life—it brings it home,” explains Kim Amey, chief of staff at the Science Center. “It becomes more relevant.”
Photo: John SChisler
At a June event, attendees submitted their thoughts on Allegheny County’s climate initiative.
The museums are going out into communities as well to engage the public on climate change issues. Science Center staff have developed live programming at community events, using interactive tools like a giant Jenga tower as an analog for the energy demands of artificial intelligence data centers. Meanwhile, the Museum of Natural History’s partnership with the county builds on more than a decade of research through two grant-funded initiatives—Climate and Urban Systems Partnership, and the related-program Climate and Rural Systems Partnership—in which Heller and her colleagues went out into both rural and urban areas of western Pennsylvania to develop better strategies for having these discussions.
They learned that it’s not enough to share information on what we know about climate change—it requires listening, too. Doing so creates a conversation—not a science lecture—and prevents emotions, such as anger, from getting in the way of learning.
“I can have a dialogue where I can share my expertise, but it’s a two-way conversation,” Heller says. “I can share my expertise in a way that’s relevant to what this person really cares about.”
Genuine Conversations
Heller and Lyon are now sharing those lessons learned with county staff as they go out into communities over the next few months to collect feedback on the Climate Action Plan.
At the county’s June event, one strategy is simply to collect public thoughts on climate change first, before engaging in conversation. Around the room, attendees wrote their ideas on sticky notes and placed them on posters that showed goals to fight global climate change in particular sectors, such as transportation, electricity, and buildings.
Hana Uman, who serves on the board of Grow Pittsburgh, an organization supporting local food initiatives such as community gardens, was among many people who wanted to encourage more composting.
“We have so much vacant land,” Uman told Heller. “Composting is not expensive, and food waste is the No. 1 material that goes into our waste stream.”
Heller nodded, listening intently, then handed her a sticky note and encouraged her to explain more.
She wasn’t the only person concerned about food waste. Other notes questioned how the county could “ease the permitting process for composters” and adopt “policies that require composting and recycling.”
We want to be a supportive partner so that the other community groups and government partners can be successful in their work. And that’s really this notion of collaborative leadership.
Nicole Heller , curator of Anthropocene Studies, Carnegie Museum of Natural History
Emily Steinberg, who recently graduated from Chatham University with a degree in environmental science, wrote about her concerns for both food waste and plastic waste. But she had trouble identifying the most appropriate poster for it because each topic was isolated, without space to explore their intersections. She wanted to talk with someone about it. So, Steinberg told Heller that the county should look at the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals as an example of a more integrated, connected set of environmental goals.
“All these different systems—transportation and our electricity, waste and food systems—are interconnected,” Steinberg says.
Photo: John SChisler
Nicole Heller (right) responds to questions at an Allegheny County Climate Action Plan event.
Heller listened, nodding in agreement. As an ecologist, Heller studies the connections among all life-forms and systems. Showing the intersections of the problems communities face, from environmental hazards to social welfare issues, might help many residents connect the dots, Heller notes. So, she shared Steinberg’s feedback with county officials in a debrief meeting afterward.
“We want to be a supportive partner so that the other community groups and government partners can be successful in their work,” Heller says. “And that’s really this notion of collaborative leadership.”
Updating Infrastructure to Meet the Moment
Carnegie Museums is also working to reduce its own footprint on the environment.
Commercial buildings were responsible for 16% of all carbon emissions in Allegheny County in 2024, according to the county’s inventory. Recent technological advancements have helped improve energy efficiency in buildings. Still, there are barriers to retrofitting older buildings to meet the highest environmental standards. New building construction gives designers the greatest breadth of control over their environmental impact, says Melissa Simonetti, director of construction and project management for Carnegie Museums.
“A lot of those green initiatives have to be baked in at the start of design,” Simonetti explains.
The Andy Warhol Museum is making sustainability a central focus for its own Pop District expansion plans. Slated to open in 2028, The Warhol’s new Creative Arts Center will house a 900-seat performance venue, and planners are working with architects, engineers, and a sustainability consultant to make it eligible for a LEED Silver eco-friendly rating. The building will include local, high-quality materials and landscaping composed of native and regional plants, according to the museum’s planning summary.
The LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) process, developed by the U.S. Green Building Council, is one of the foremost green building rating systems. It considers factors such as energy use, water efficiency, indoor air quality, and materials. While buildings must acquire 40 points under this system to become “LEED Certified,” LEED Silver requires at least 10 extra points.
Nearby, the Science Center’s PPG Science Pavilion is certified LEED Gold. Built in 2018, the four-story, 48,000-square-foot expansion earned more than 60 points toward certification for features such as an energy-efficient building envelope and low-flow plumbing fixtures.
The Science Center is now designing a new sustainable infrastructure for its North Lot. A photovoltaic canopy with 1,600 solar panels will cover most of the surface. Next to it, a science park with no admission cost will help the Science Center present science content to more community members, while also introducing green space into a landscape that is mostly asphalt. Adding greenery to dense concentrations of pavement, buildings, and other surfaces helps to combat the urban heat island effect, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The solar panels will help power the museum, saving an estimated $20,000 per month in electricity costs and reducing the Science Center’s carbon emissions by 1,000 metric tons per year, explains Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., director of Kamin Science Center and vice president of Carnegie Museums.
Carnegie Museums has worked to reduce its own climate footprint by improving the energy efficiency of its buildings and by making sustainability a focus for new construction.
“It’s not just one part of our mission. It’s education. It’s technology, It’s futuristic thinking. And it’s sustainability,” Brown says. “We should be a model for how technology can function for the benefit of humanity.”
Brown notes that information about how the solar panels function and what they achieve will be an important addition on-site. He hopes Science Center visitors will be inspired to pursue renewable energy in their homes and businesses.
“The worst thing we can do is tell people a problem and not give them ideas or hope on how they can be a part of addressing it,” Brown says.
Modernizing Carnegie Museums’ historic Oakland campus presents a whole different challenge, particularly in the original part of the building that dates back 131 years, Simonetti notes. Still, she says incremental changes have helped reduce its energy usage. Energy-efficient LED lights have replaced incandescent bulbs, and building insulation has been improved to save energy.
In 2009, the Bellefield Boiler Plant (commonly known as “The Cloud Factory”), a central steam plant that provides heat and hot water to much of the Oakland neighborhood, was converted from coal to natural gas, reducing emissions by almost two-thirds, according to an inventory submitted to the federal government. Natural gas contributes to climate change, but at a lower rate than coal.
Facility managers at Carnegie Museums continue to work toward fully transitioning to renewable energy, but some obstacles have slowed progress.
In their current form, available solar panels were too heavy to place on the roof of the century-old Museum of Natural History, explains Tony Young, chair of the operating committee for the Bellefield Boiler Plant and former vice president of facilities, planning, and operations for Carnegie Museums. Another idea—purchasing renewable energy credits—did not come to fruition after several private energy-generation projects failed to secure approvals and connect to Pennsylvania’s energy grid, he explains.
As technology improves and the region collectively develops more ways for businesses and institutions to reduce their emissions, leaders at Carnegie Museums say more progress should be expected.“We want to be here for the next generation, so it’s important to integrate modern climate controls, sustainable building tech, and energy-efficient systems when we can,” says Simonetti.
Collectively, these investments in infrastructure, exhibitions, partnerships, and public outreach tell a story of the many ways museums can and should be a leader in addressing global issues at a time when political strife has stalled progress.
Heller says she wants to continue working with the county on other climate-related initiatives, and encourages other institutions to join them. “Part of what motivates me to build these civic partnerships is the opportunity to put a spotlight on the work and help people be informed about what is really happening in our community.” she says. “I think that’s a really important role for a museum.”

title: Crawling from the collections - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Crawling from the collections
Two amateur spider enthusiasts at Carnegie Museum of Natural History discovered a new species hidden within its archive of arachnids—and named it for John Denver.
By Jason Bittel
Fall 2026
Behind the Scenes
Science & Nature
Print
A
Photo: Valerie Warhol
When scientists announce the discovery of a new species, people often imagine adventurers wading through swamps or clinging to the side of a mountain. But sometimes—in fact, a lot of the time—the remains of a creature no one has ever seen before aren’t waiting to be discovered at the end of the world. They’re sitting in a jar of preservative, tucked inside a museum drawer, surrounded by specimens that haven’t moved in decades.
That is, until someone like Valerie Warhol or Amy Bianco comes along.
Warhol (no relation to Andy) is an informatics assistant and Bianco a part-time volunteer at Carnegie Museum of Natural History. Though their work together may seem mundane to some, they serve an absolutely critical purpose.
“We’re mostly just trying to go through specimens that nobody’s looked at and identify as much old stuff as possible and get it digitized and cataloged,” says Warhol, who specializes in arachnids.
Digitizing natural history collections is vital for advancing research. By digging into museum cabinets and converting physical specimens and their labels into high-resolution images and data, Bianco and Warhol are helping to make parts of the collections accessible to researchers around the world, potentially leading to new scientific insights and discoveries. The task is enormous, as the museum is home to 18 million invertebrate specimens alone, which makes the collection one of the largest in the country.
“And only about 1% is digitized,” Warhol explains.
And so it was in spring 2025 that Warhol and Bianco were going through the arachnid collection, identifying specimens one by one, when they landed on a jar with four rusty-orange trapdoor spiders curled up inside.
“We thought, either it’s a major range extension for one of the known species, or it’s something that nobody knows about yet.”
Amy Bianco, part-time volunteer at Carnegie Museum of Natural History
Bianco remembers being particularly excited because it was a type of spider she’d never seen outside of a field guide. Sometimes called Oreo cookie spiders, these types of trapdoor spiders have a large, flattened rump full of ridges that can be used to prevent predators from attacking them in the tunnels they inhabit.
When Bianco used a taxonomic key to determine the mystery spider’s genus,
Cyclocosmia
, she realized that the species on record were only known to be from Mexico and the American South. However, the specimen in hand was caught in West Virginia in 1994.
“And so we thought, either it’s a major range extension for one of the known species, or it’s something that nobody knows about yet,” says Bianco, a lifelong spider enthusiast who also writes a blog on the subject and leads community workshops about arachnids in western Pennsylvania.
What’s more, when Warhol used another key to try to advance the identification from genus to species, something that required painstaking counting of the rump ridges under magnification, they learned that the count didn’t sync up with any known species of
Cyclocosmia
.
Bianco and Warhol knew they needed backup, so they reached out to Danniella Sherwood, a biologist with the Arachnology Research Association in the United Kingdom. Sherwood had recently described a new species of trapdoor spider in Vietnam, which meant she was more familiar with the genus than most experts. Fortunately, Sherwood knew what feature to look at next.
“According to Dr. Sherwood, there was a little knob on the pedipalps that appeared to be distinct for the species,” says Bianco.
In spiders, pedipalps appear as two tiny legs near the mouth, and they’re useful for manipulating food.
“They’re also very commonly used as windshield wipers,” says Bianco. “A lot of times they have like little brushes on them that they use to clean their eyes, which is so cute!”
Interestingly, when male spiders reach sexual maturity, their pedipalps transform into reproductive structures that assist in the transfer of sperm. Best of all, a male’s pedipalps are often unique to its species, like keys that only fit into a special kind of lock. And, using ultramagnified photographs provided by Bianco and Warhol, Sherwood was able to confirm that the orange spider’s palps were unlike any other trapdoor spider’s on record. Given the locale where the new critters were found, she suggested naming the species after the late, great John Denver.
Cyclocosmia johndenveri
became an official species at the publication of its official description in the science journal
Natura Somogyiensis
, with Bianco and Warhol even included as co-authors on the paper. And yet, some mystery about the specimen still remains.
“We still don’t have a female for the species,” says Warhol. “There isn’t a ton of spider research going on in West Virginia, so we’re hoping someday someone will take a picture of one and put it on iNaturalist. You never know, you could be contributing something valuable to science or leading to a new discovery!”
Jason Bittel is a National Geographic Explorer and author of
Grizzled: Love Letters to 50 of North America’s Least Understood Animals
(National Geographic Books 2026).

title: Behind the Scenes at the Museum - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Behind the Scenes at the Museum
New tours offer the public rare access to the Museum of Natural History’s scientists, specimens, and conservation work that underpin the exhibitions.
By Aakanksha Agarwal
Fall 2026
Behind the Scenes
Science & Nature
Print
A
Paleobiology Collections Manager Sarah Davis leads a tour of vertebrate paleontology specimens. Photo: Aakanksha Agarwal
Whispers rippled through the group of 10 museumgoers as they followed Paleobiology Collections Manager Sarah Davis into the basement of Carnegie Museum of Natural History. They’re about to explore a part of the museum that few visitors ever get to see.
“This feels clandestine,” one visitor exclaims.
A heavy metal door swings shut, muffling the galleries above into near silence. Beyond it lies the Big Bone Room, where rows of compact shelving stretch into the distance, oversized dinosaur fossils rest on pallets, and worktables are outfitted with microscopes, cameras, and computers. Here and in the Little Bone Room across the hall (named for the size of the room, not the size of the specimens), almost everything in the museum’s vertebrate paleontology collection is stored—from dinosaurs and ancient reptiles to fossilized birds and mammals.
“I often think of the collections as a library of the history of life,” says Davis. But unlike most other libraries, this one isn’t traditionally open to the public.
Earlier this year, the museum began offering its adult visitors (age 18+) behind-the-scenes tours of spaces that include the vertebrate paleontology collection, the museum’s herbarium, and the historic “Alcohol House” where preserved amphibians and reptiles are kept. The response was overwhelmingly positive, says Sarah Crawford, the museum’s senior director of museum experience. The first four tours were offered to groups of 10 visitors this spring during NatureFest, the museum’s annual celebration of the natural world, and tickets sold out within 24 hours. A second round of tours offered during DinoFest, the museum’s summer paleontology festival, also sold out.
The museum is still working out details on the price, future content, and frequency of the tours. Beyond being a potential revenue stream, this program also is an opportunity for the museum to deepen its relationship with patrons, Crawford explains.
“In exhibitions, we’re often translators,” she says. “We’re the people standing between the public and the scientist. We thought if we could remove that barrier and bring the public directly to the scientists and the collections, it would hit home in a much more powerful way.”
Researchers, university classes, and donors have long visited the collections, Crawford says. But, for most visitors, the museum’s scientific work remains largely unseen.
“We thought if we could remove that barrier and bring the public directly to the scientists and the collections, it would hit home in a much more powerful way.”
Sarah Crawford, senior director of museum experience at Carnegie Museum of Natural History
The dinosaurs upstairs represent only a fraction of the collection, Davis says. The museum’s three paleontology collections combined contain close
to 1 million fossil specimens, from vertebrates and invertebrates to fossil plants.
Not every specimen belongs in an exhibition, Davis explains. Some are too fragile or scientifically important to display. Others consist of little more than a single vertebra or fragment of limb.
“The fossilized end of a bird’s ankle bone is incredibly exciting to me,” she says. “But it’s tiny, and might not look like much. It takes a lot more interpretation to explain why that’s important.”
A few racks over, Davis shows the group several neck and back vertebrae from the original
Diplodocus carnegii
—aka “Dippy”—that aren’t part of the mounted specimen upstairs. She recounts how Andrew Carnegie, eager to create a world-class museum, sent an expedition west after reading an 1890s newspaper story about a giant dinosaur discovered in Wyoming. That search eventually led to the discovery of the famous specimen whose casts would travel the world while the original fossil became Pittsburgh’s crown jewel.
The museum also houses another celebrity: the holotype, or specimen first scientifically named, of
Tyrannosaurus rex
, purchased in 1941 for $7,000 after help from donors.
Standing before the
T. rex
fossil, Davis points to healed bite marks and signs of infection on its lower jaw. “It’s important to remember every specimen was once an individual animal that lived its own life,” she says. “It represents its species, but it also represents its own experiences.”
The behind-the-scenes tours extend well beyond paleontology. In the Alcohol House, visitors explore amphibian and reptile collections with Curator of Herpetology Jen Sheridan. In the herbarium, Curator of Botany Mason Heberling introduces tour groups to more than 550,000 preserved plant specimens, some collected in western Pennsylvania more than two centuries ago.
“People sometimes think museum collections are simply archives of old objects,” Heberling says. “In reality, they’re active research tools.”
Heberling and his college interns compare historical specimens with modern ones, documenting introduced species, shifting biodiversity, and plants flowering earlier due to warmer spring weather. Comparing two specimens collected a century apart helps make a conversation about climate change more tangible.
“Biodiversity is dynamic,” Heberling says. “Because we have these collections, we have a baseline. They aren’t just telling us about the past. They’re helping us understand our present and our future.”
The tours have become a source of discovery for Davis, too. Each group sees the collections through a different lens. Architecture students notice details biology students miss, while others gravitate toward unexpected specimens. “They remind me my job isn’t typical,” she says. “They make me see the collection differently.”

title: Q+A: Amy Covell-Murthy - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Q+A: Amy Covell-Murthy
In conversation with the collection manager of archaeology at Carnegie Museum of Natural History.
By Chris Fleisher
Fall 2026
Facetime Q&A
Science & Nature
Print
A
Photo: Joashua Franzos
Natural history museums have long sought to tell the stories of people from around the world, but in recent years there’s been a shift in how they go about telling them.
Today, Carnegie Museum of Natural History and many of its peers aim to share authority with the communities they portray while caring for cultural artifacts in the museum collections. Amy Covell-Murthy, the museum’s collection manager of archaeology, is helping the institution do that.
In her 19 years at the the museum, Covell-Murthy has carefully built close relationships with Indigenous communities. She continues to repatriate sacred objects and artifacts with human remains that are contained in the museum’s collections—as required under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act—and consults with tribal members on how best to care for the items that remain in the museum’s care. She also worked with members of the Quapaw Nation to co-develop the
Keeping Traditions Alive
exhibition in the Alcoa Foundation Hall of American Indians.
Holding a bachelor’s degree in anthropology and master’s in museum studies, Covell-Murthy is still learning how museums can build more equitable relationships with communities from around the globe. In June, she returned from a trip to England, where over the course of eight weeks she learned about the University of Oxford’s community-led museum practices as part of the William T. Hillman Visiting Fellowship program, a new collaboration between Oxford’s Gardens, Libraries, and Museums and Carnegie Museums.
Sharing authority with outside groups is delicate and challenging work, she notes, but ultimately helps the institution be a better steward of the objects in its care, as well as the human stories it presents.
“Having a person-first mentality rather than an object-first mentality has been really important,” Covell-Murthy says.
Q: What did you learn at Oxford that you want to bring back to the museum?
A:
I’d say, when working on completely community-driven programming, it’s OK to not have a really clear end goal. You can have a perfectly wonderful program that just starts out with everyone brainstorming and figuring out along the way what something’s going to look like in the end.
Q: When did you first become aware of issues around repatriation in museum collections?
A:
Twenty years ago, people didn’t really talk about human remains in museum collections because everyone was worried that they would get in trouble. At some point, I realized that it was something that shouldn’t be hidden and that we all should be talking about it. That’s when I switched the focus of my career from objects to people, reminding myself that the people in our care, the human remains in our care, are people with cultural and family ties.
Q: Partnering with Indigenous communities is a critical part of this work. How do you ensure that it’s a genuine partnership?
A:
How to make relationships not extractive and sustainable is something that we’re constantly trying to do better. We’ve worked with multiple Indigenous communities—the Quapaw and the Fort Peck tribes, for example—in a reciprocal way in which we co-curate exhibits with them, and people are paid for their time. We have started asking the question, “What do you want the people of Pittsburgh to know about your community?” instead of the other way around. We are also in the habit now of going out into the communities instead of always asking them to come here.
Q: You’ve noted that in anthropology, the aim is to allow communities to tell authentic personal stories. How does a museum do that?
A:
In the past, an exhibit would have a goal to teach visitors something. Now, the goal of authentic stories and first-person stories is to bring people together, to make it so that you can see the similarities and the differences between our cultures and not see these people as others or outsiders. We all have a lot in common. I think that it’s easier to reach people on a personal level than it is when we have an exhibit that’s not focused on the human experience.
Q: How do you collect those personal stories?
A:
The
Keeping Traditions Alive
exhibit is the first-person account of two Quapaw elders who were able to choose the theme of the exhibit. Betty, one of the elders who’s featured, made the dress and the ceramics that are featured in the exhibit. We purchased those items from her after asking what she thought would fit in the collection in Pittsburgh the best. Those were the things that she chose for us to purchase from her. The purpose was to give people in Pittsburgh a glimpse into the community that these Quapaw elders are a part of.
Q: What lessons have you learned doing this work?
A:
You can’t expect everyone to function on your timeline. You have to be able to go with the flow and the tone that they set. My biggest thing is that we’re gonna make a lot of mistakes, and we have to own up to those mistakes and always do better.

title: All Together ... We Enlighten  - Carnegie Magazine
text:
All Together … We Enlighten
A philanthropic leader wants to support STEM opportunities for kids in Pittsburgh.
By Chris Fleisher
Fall 2026
All Together
Print
A
Who:
Myah Moore Irick
What She supports:
Kamin Science Center summer camps
Why it matters:
“STEM is the language of our future economy.”
The Hawaiian island of O‘ahu is often pictured as paradise, and for Myah Moore Irick it was also the foundation for a journey defined by curiosity, determination, and a passion for learning.
Raised in a more rural part of the island, Irick grew up surrounded by natural beauty and a close-knit community. While opportunities to visit museums, travel widely, or access cultural institutions were limited, those experiences helped spark a desire to explore the world beyond her hometown.
That opportunity came at age 17, when she left Hawaii to attend college in Portland, Oregon. The move opened new doors and broadened her perspective, setting her on a path of lifelong learning and achievement. Since then, Irick has traveled extensively, earned advanced degrees from prestigious institutions including Columbia University and Brown University, and obtained her financial planning certification through Northwestern University. She also founded The Irick Group, part of Merrill Private Wealth Management, where she is senior vice president and private wealth advisor based in Pittsburgh.
Looking back, Irick credits her upbringing with helping shape the perspective, work ethic, and appreciation for opportunity that continue to guide her today. Now, she reflects on the educational opportunities available to her own three children, and how they’ll be shaped by access to the city’s museums and cultural institutions. And she wants other youth in Pittsburgh to have access to them, too.
“It’s really deepened my commitment to institutions like the Kamin Science Center, and Carnegie Museums as a whole,” she says.
Since moving to Pittsburgh in 2019, Irick has become increasingly involved as a philanthropic leader in the city, and particularly with Carnegie Museums.
Irick serves on the board of Kamin Science Center and established an endowment with her husband to support scholarships for underserved youth to attend Science Center summer camps. She is also a co-chair of Carnegie Museums’ ALL TOGETHER comprehensive campaign, which will raise funds to enhance museum operations, exhibitions and educational programming, and collaborations and strategic partnerships that amplify their reach on the local, national, and global stages.
Irick is particularly keen to provide more STEM-education opportunities for local youth.
“I feel like STEM is the language of our future economy,” she says. “We talk a lot about artificial intelligence, but we also have to think much more broadly about that. Many underserved communities are excluded from the conversation. When that happens and we cut out an entire portion of our population, we slow our collective growth and we miss out on unique skills and perspectives.”
Irick recalls developing science fair projects as a kid, most of them inspired by her own experiences. She grew up with asthma and didn’t have access to quality health services, so many of her projects were around respiratory issues.
She wonders what topics she might have explored were there a science center to inspire her.
“I always came up with my own projects,” she explains. “But I can only imagine that if I had access to the Science Center or more science educators what that would look like.”
Even as an adult, Irick takes inspiration from the Science Center, whether revisiting a longtime personal favorite—the historic Miniature Railroad & Village® —or learning STEM concepts at the newly opened Science of Speed. She’s impressed by the Science Center’s exhibits and programming for visitors of all ages, and it’s become a regular destination for her entire family.
Irick enjoys watching her kids’ worlds open wider with each visit. And she wants as many youth to experience that as well. It is, she believes, essential for creating a richer, more equitable, and more sustainable world.
“These are their futures,” she says. “What is the kind of world that I want them to live in? What will they inherit?”
Learn more about how you can support your museums through the ALL TOGETHER campaign
.

title: Closer Look: Search for Life - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Closer Look: Search for Life
A new perspective on familiar offerings at Carnegie Museums.
Fall 2026
Science & Nature
STEM
Print
A
Photo: Becky Thurner
On a
bitterly cold Thursday afternoon in February 2021
, 40 socially distanced visitors gathered at the Buhl Planetarium to watch space history.
They were viewing a live feed as NASA’s newest rover
made its descent toward the Mars surface. Named “Perseverance,” the rover was the “most advanced robotic explorer ever sent to the red planet,” according to NASA, but its safe landing was far from certain. After 7 minutes of anxious silence,
the group of strangers
rejoiced—jumping up and down and cheering. Perseverance’s wheels were set on Martian soil, where it would join its older rover companion, Curiosity.
The following year, guests would be able to pilot their own two rovers across the red planet’s rocky terrain as part of
Mars: The Next Giant Leap
at Kamin Science Center, giving visitors in Pittsburgh just a taste of the challenge that the NASA rovers had ahead of them. The mission for both the real-life Mars rovers and those at the Science Center was the same: to find underground water sources and evidence of ancient life.
“It’s similar to paleontology, but rover-style,” says Jessi Sedon, associate director of exhibits support and digital experiences at Kamin Science Center.
Several billion years ago, the dusty and cold red desert was once much warmer and covered in flowing bodies of water, according to
NASA
. Rovers scan the terrain below using X-ray fluorescence, environmental sensors, and ground-penetrating radar to uncover what remains. Their findings report underground ice as Mars’ only water form, and the possibility of organic molecules, the chemical foundation of life.
The aim of the Science Center’s rovers is to model the process vital to human life on Mars: exploration. The two vehicles operate wirelessly, just like the pair on Mars. Using a joystick mounted on the exhibit’s information display, users search the rocky, ruddy surface for tiny spots that represent organic molecules. The challenge of keeping the rovers from crashing into each other demonstrates the difficulty of navigating the Mars terrain.
“Trying to get them to move and function and work around each other demonstrates how hard it can be,” Sedon says. “I couldn’t imagine doing this with an actual rover on Mars.”
As Sedon troubleshoots technology challenges with the Science Center rovers,
NASA continues to do the same with the real-life Perseverance
. Just last year, NASA announced it had discovered a rock containing potential biosignatures—clues that suggest past life may have been present 200 million miles away from planet Earth.

Seen + Heard: Fall 2026
In brief, what’s new around the museums.
Fall 2026
Where Art & Science Meet
Print
A
The Warhol Welcomes a New Curator
Hannah Klemm has joined The Andy Warhol Museum as its Milton Fine Curator of Art. She was most recently curator of modern and contemporary art at the Blanton Museum of Art at the University of Texas at Austin. “What has always inspired me about both Warhol and the museum is a belief that art does not happen in isolation,” Klemm says.“It emerges through communities, conversations, and the exchange of ideas.” Klemm also served as associate curator of modern and contemporary art for the Saint Louis Art Museum.
Photo: Manny Alcala
Fourth Annual Call for Art That Imagines an Equitable Pittsburgh
Carnegie Museums is inviting local artists of all ages to imagine what it means to make a home in Pittsburgh where everyone can live and thrive. The museums and its partners—Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, the University of Pittsburgh, and Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh—announced the fourth annual “Envisioning a Just Pittsburgh” call for art. Submissions are due by Nov. 1. More information can be found at www.carnegiemuseums. org/JustPgh.
And the Award Goes To …
Carnegie
Magazine!
Carnegie
magazine took home three wins in this year’s Golden Quill awards for excellence in journalism, including best in show for the magazine division! The magazine’s spring 2025 cover story, “Chirps in the Night,” about herpetologist Jen Sheridan’s exploits in the Bornean rainforest claimed the top prize for profile writing, as well as the Ray Sprigle Memorial Award for the best overall magazine story. The award for education writing went to “Printmaking with Purpose” about the teen printmaking programs at The Andy Warhol Museum.
Carnegie
magazine was also awarded first place for education writing at this year’s Pittsburgh Black Media Federation banquet for “Nurturing Empowerment,” about the Museum of Art’s Empowered Educators program.
New Dinosaur Species Identified
Illustration: Lewis LaRosa, colorized by Jão Canola.
Carnegie Museum of Natural History’s senior paleontologist, Matt Lamanna, has helped identify a new species of dinosaur found in China. Lamanna co-authored a paper that revealed the new species, named
Jian changmaensis
. The microraptor is the first non-avian dinosaur to be found at one of the most important fossil bird sites in the world, the Changma Basin of northwestern China. The predatory
Jian
fed on prehistoric birds and other small animals, and gives researchers a new perspective on the Age of Dinosaurs in that region.
“It’s emotional. It’s a beautiful exhibit. But there’s a lot of new stories to tell. That’s part of our duty also, I believe, to show that science is changing and we continue to learn.”
Sarah Crawford, director of museum experience at Carnegie Museum of Natural History, to the
Pittsburgh Post-Gazette
on the closing of the Polar World exhibition
Charles ‘Teenie’ Harris joins Pittsburgh Walk of Fame
Legendary Pittsburgh photographer Charles “Teenie” Harris will join Andrew Carnegie and Andy Warhol on Pittsburgh’s Walk of Fame. The Strip District landmark, which had its debut last year, honors notable individuals with ties to the Pittsburgh region. Harris chronicled Pittsburgh’s Black community from the 1930s to the ‘80s, and his archive of more than 70,000 images and photonegatives is owned and preserved by Carnegie Museum of Art. Harris officially will be inducted during a ceremony at The Terminal on Oct. 13.

title: President's Note: Fall 2026 - Carnegie Magazine
text:
President’s Note: Fall 2026
A message from Steven Knapp.
Fall 2026
Print
A
Photo: Joshua Franzos
Above and beyond anything else they are or do, museums like ours are repositories of objects and experiences that connect their visitors with the inspiring achievements of human creativity and the wondrous evolution of the universe and our planet as science continues to explore it. Those experiences are more than entertaining; they amount to a kind of learning that is very different from the formal schooling provided by institutions of elementary, secondary, and higher education. Call it, for want of a better term,
informal
education.
At Carnegie Museums, informal education takes many different forms that extend beyond the fundamental experience of a visitor stirred by an encounter with a brilliant artwork or a stunning fossil. Our four museums constantly seek ways to extend their educational mission through innovative work with schools, community groups, and families. Hundreds of thousands of young people benefit every year, many through out-of-school experiences like field trips and summer camps.
“Our four museums constantly seek ways to extend their educational mission through innovative work with schools, community groups, and families. Hundreds of thousands of young people benefit every year.”
Studies show that museums improve young people’s ability to learn and help them to build confidence in their own interests and abilities. Renowned artist and Pittsburgh native Sharif Bey was a self-described “museum kid from Beltzhoover” whose curiosity led him through the galleries of Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History. He eventually signed up for the Museum of Art’s Saturday art classes, like other famed Pittsburgh-born and -bred artists before him, including Andy Warhol and Raymond Saunders. Through October 12 at The Andy Warhol Museum, you can enjoy an exhibition of his monumental ceramic sculptures, aptly titled
Sharif Bey: Homecoming
.
John Grayson didn’t grow up as a “museum kid,” but years ago, as a C-average student at his McKeesport elementary school, his experience at a Science Center workshop led him to earn first place at a robotics challenge by programming a robot to negotiate a maze, a task he and a partner completed in a record 25 minutes. On the bus ride home, he told his teacher, “I didn’t know my brain worked that way.” He went on to become an A student in his school’s Academy of Math and Science program.
In this issue, you’ll read about wealth manager Myah Moore Irick, who serves on Kamin Science Center’s advisory board and is a co-chair of Carnegie Museums’ ALL TOGETHER Campaign. Myah grew up surrounded by natural beauty in rural Hawaii but had limited access to museums. She recounts her experience coming up with childhood science projects without access to a science museum, and she wonders what topics she might have explored if there had been a science center to inspire her. She looks forward to seeing the ways her own three children will be shaped by their access to the rich informal education Carnegie Museums provides.

title: From the Archives: An interview with Sally Dixon - Carnegie Magazine
text:
From the Archives: An interview with Sally Dixon
Items from the magazine’s century of archives.
Carnegie Magazine
Fall 2026
Art
Print
A
Editor’s note:
The following exchange appeared in the October 1973 issue of Carnegie magazine, just a few years into the tenure of Sally Dixon, who founded the film department at Carnegie Museum of Art in 1970 and was its first curator. The interview was conducted by Robert J. Gangewere, longtime editor of the magazine. In the original publication, the interview was presented as a “shooting script,” with notes about how a filmmaker might film the interview. That layout can be seen in full on the magazine’s online archive page.
Robert J. Gangewere:
So you were not always oriented towards film as an art form?
Sally Dixon
: My whole background was art. Even in my earliest memories I had the desire to be an artist. I was always an art major at school. At home I had my room, my studio. Line and light were my great concerns, and the rhythms produced by them. As a child I always drew or painted. But I would not call myself an artist…rather a putterer, in more or less concentration. When I was young my family moved a lot. Nineteen times in 21 years. We lived in San Francisco, New York, Washington D.C., Detroit, Pittsburgh, many places within those areas.
Gangewere:
Then you’ve experienced many cities as a worker and artist. Is Pittsburgh a number one choice for a place to be?
Dixon:
Wherever your heart is is a good place to be.
Gangewere:
That sounds like a diplomatic answer.
Dixon:
But I don’t mean it diplomatically, I mean it practically. I love this city. To me there’s an excitement, a sense of vitality here. People say, “What do you mean…it’s dead.” Not for me it isn’t.
Gangewere:
I know what you mean. Perhaps it’s a mix of things—the working class tradition, the new technocrats, the administrative centers, lots of university people, young people. If you put it all together in a medium-sized city you can get in touch with every aspect of it.
Dixon:
I do have a sense of encompassing in my mind the whole city. I have the sense of knowing what’s going on here and what the possibilities are which are endless…I really like it. Also, just visually, the city of Pittsburgh is beautiful. This has been a real plus for filmmakers. Their whole life is seeing. Their art, their business, is seeing. They come through the Fort Pitt tunnel from the airport…ahh…they say. The textures thrill them. Pittsburgh will always have its rivers, its trees, its textures. It can never be wall-to-wall concrete. It’s broken by rivers and cliffs. You’ve got ancient ratty crumbling ghettos next to an expensive throbbing metropolitan city, and a few minutes away you’ve got a cultural and academic center. A filmmaker doesn’t have to drive for miles to get to a different mood, a different topography, a different economic situation or lifestyle. And the city has that tum-of-the-century Victorian style—what’s called “Pittsburgh architecture.” And that’s exciting too. When the filmmakers say “ahh,” that confirms it for me. I never knew before if I liked it because of my own subjective feelings about coming home to it. But the artists sense the vitality here. Right now. Something is brewing.
Gangewere:
A wave of creativity in filmmaking, you mean?
Dixon:
Yes. This happened here once before. At the turn of the century. It happened nowhere else. The nickelodeon had been trying to happen in a number of cities and did not come off—but it came off here. I have the sense that there is a thrust in filmmaking, a whole wave, right now, and that it’s breaking through in Pittsburgh and in other cities. And I have that sense about my job right now. That I’m in the right spot at the right time. That I’m part of something larger than a personally satisfying job.

October 1973 issue of
Carnegie
magazine
.

For more than 46 years, Albert Kollar was collection manager of invertebrate paleontology at Carnegie Museum of Natural History. He was always eager to share his knowledge with the public, and one of his favorite things to do was to spend a day answering visitors’ questions about the museum’s collections and their own geological discoveries. Albert passed away unexpectedly at the age of 72 on April 9, 2024.

Big Picture
The Andy Warhol Museum unveiled a major public art installation in June, titled Anatomy of the Human, as part of its Pop District initiative. The mural was created by artist Mikael Owunna, who drew inspiration from African cosmologies and Warhol’s use of multiple silkscreens to produce stop-motion-style images. The artwork is located across from the museum in Pop Park on East General Robinson Street.
